readerTitle: When is it worth finding out more before you decide?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (브런치 메뉴를 고민하는 식당, 온보딩 이메일을 테스트하는 소프트웨어 팀) + 실제 연구 개념 (Howard의 정보 가치 이론, Hubbard의 측정 역설). 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 정보의 가치는 얼마나 정확한가가 아니라, 그 정보가 내 결정을 바꿀 수 있는가로 정해진다.
misconception: 정보는 많을수록 좋고, 조사를 더 하면 언제나 더 나은 결정을 한다.

sources.text: Howard, R. A. (1966). Information Value Theory. IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics, 2(1), 22–26.
Hubbard, D. W. How to Measure Anything: Finding the Value of Intangibles in Business ("measurement inversion")
모든 사업 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 계산 확인: 설문이 결정을 바꿀 확률 10% × 바꿨을 때 아끼는 돈 $4,000 = $400. 설문이 완벽히 정확하다고 가정한 상한선이며, 설문 가격 $3,000보다 훨씬 낮습니다. 모두 가상 수치입니다.
Hubbard의 'measurement inversion'(조직이 가치가 낮은 것을 많이 측정하고 가치가 높은 것은 덜 측정하는 경향)은 책의 관찰을 일반적으로만 서술했습니다. 구체적 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다. 게시 전 원문 표현을 확인하세요.
Howard(1966) 논문이 정보 가치를 의사결정 분석의 틀로 정리한 초기 문헌이라는 점을 서지 정보와 함께 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: The weather check that changed nothing
body: You check the forecast before leaving home. It says 20% chance of rain. You take your jacket, like you do every day.
The check felt useful. But if you'd have taken the jacket either way, it was worth exactly nothing. That idea matters far more when the check costs $3,000.

image.label: Person checking a phone forecast while already holding a jacket
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 현관에서 한 손에는 이미 재킷을 든 사람이 다른 손으로 휴대폰 날씨 화면을 보고 있음. 화면에는 구름 아이콘과 "20%". 실제 앱 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A research firm offers a $3,000 survey.
body: You run a neighborhood restaurant and plan to add weekend brunch. A research firm offers to survey 400 locals about brunch demand. It costs $3,000 and takes six weeks.
Before deciding whether to buy it, what should you ask first?

options.text: How many people will they survey, and how?
options.feedback: Quality matters, but only after you know the answer could matter. A perfect survey is still a waste if it can't change your plan.

options.text: Is there any result that would make me drop the brunch plan?
options.feedback: This tells you whether the survey can change your decision at all. If no answer would stop you, it's worth little at any price.

options.text: Can I get the same survey for less?
options.feedback: A cheaper survey saves money on the price tag. But you still haven't asked whether the information is worth anything to you.

cards.title: What could the survey save you?
body: Be honest: you'd only cancel brunch if the survey came back very negative. You guess there's a 10% chance of that. If brunch flopped, you'd lose about $4,000 before noticing and stopping.
Even a perfect survey is worth about **$400** to you. It costs $3,000.

breakdown.label: Chance it changes your plan
breakdown.detail: Only a very bad result would stop you

breakdown.label: Saved if it does
breakdown.detail: The loss from a flop you'd avoid

cards.title: The value of more information
body: **The value of information** is how much better your decision gets because you learned something. If no possible answer would change what you do, the value is zero.
Three things raise it: how unsure you really are, how much money is at stake, and how hard a wrong choice is to undo. Decision researcher Ronald Howard set out this way of thinking in a 1966 paper.

image.label: Three dials: uncertainty, stakes, reversibility
image.brief: 계기판 3개가 나란히 있는 인포그래픽. 라벨은 "How unsure?", "How much at stake?", "How hard to undo?". 세 바늘이 모두 높을 때만 가운데 "Worth finding out" 램프가 켜짐.

cards.title: Often the cheapest research is just trying it.
body: Brunch is easy to reverse. Two trial weekends cost the restaurant about $800 in extra staff and food. They show real customers paying real money, not people guessing on a form.
When a choice can be undone quickly, acting *is* the research. Save expensive studies for choices you can't take back, like signing a ten-year lease.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams face the same trade-off. A feature behind a switch you can turn off is cheap to try. A price change sent to every customer, or a database migration, is the place for careful research first.

cards.title: We measure what's easy, not what matters.
body: Measurement expert Douglas Hubbard calls it the **measurement inversion**: organizations often measure small, easy things in detail and leave their biggest uncertainties unmeasured.
A café might count every napkin while guessing about whether a second location would work. The napkin data is precise. It just never changes a big decision.

cards.title: Overconfidence makes all research look worthless.
body: This math depends on how unsure you honestly are. If you're sure you're right, nothing seems able to change your mind, so every study looks like a waste.
Ask a colleague what result would surprise them. And treat a rare outcome that could sink the business differently. Even a small chance of ruin can be worth paying to check.

cards.title: Now it's a software team.
body: Your product team wants a six-week A/B test of two subject lines for a welcome email. Whichever wins, you could switch back in minutes. The same team is also deciding whether to drop monthly billing and offer annual plans only.
Where should the testing effort go?

options.text: Run the full six-week subject-line test to be rigorous
options.feedback: You'd get a clean answer, but to a cheap, reversible question. Six weeks of attention buys very little.

options.text: Ship the subject line you prefer, watch the numbers, and test the billing change carefully
options.feedback: The billing change is uncertain, affects revenue, and is hard to undo with existing customers. That's where information pays.

options.text: Skip testing for both and move fast
options.feedback: You save time on both, but you take a big, hard-to-reverse bet on billing with no evidence.

cards.title: Information is worth what it can change.
body: Before paying for research or waiting for more data, ask which answer would make you choose differently, and how much that would save.
**Try it today:** pick one report you check every week. Write down the last decision it changed. If you can't name one, check it less.
